subject: English
topic: Error Spotting III — subject-verb agreement, tense, articles, prepositions, conjunctions
description: Identify the erroneous part of a sentence. Common errors: neither/either with singular verb, since vs for, comprising of, subjunctive mood, dangling participle, pronoun agreement. SSC CGL/IBPS PO standard.

questions.stem: Identify the error in: 'She is one of the students who is selected for the scholarship.'

options.option_text: 'who is selected' — should be 'who are selected' (antecedent = students, plural)
'She is one' — the phrase 'one of' itself is grammatically incorrect in this context
'for the scholarship' — preposition 'for' should be replaced by 'to the scholarship'
No error — the sentence is grammatically complete and entirely correct as written

questions.explanation: ERROR: The relative clause 'who is selected' modifies 'students' (the noun immediately before 'who'), not 'one.' Since 'students' is plural, the verb must be plural: 'who ARE selected.' RULE: In 'one of the [plural noun] who/that [verb],' the verb agrees with the PLURAL NOUN, not with 'one.' CORRECT: 'She is one of the students who are selected for the scholarship.' COMPARE: 'She is the only one of the students who is selected' — here 'only one' is the antecedent → singular verb IS correct. EXAM TRAP: The subject 'one' is closer to the verb 'is' and students may agree with the closer noun by proximity error. RULE: Proximity agreement is WRONG in English. Agreement follows the actual grammatical antecedent. PYQ FREQUENCY: one-of-the-plural-who errors in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, SBI PO English — 1-2× per year.

questions.stem: Identify the error in: 'He has been working in this company since three years.'

options.option_text: 'since three years' — should be 'for three years' (since = point in time; for = duration)
'has been working' — should be 'is working' as continuous tense is incorrect here
'in this company' — should be 'at this company' as 'at' is the correct preposition
No error — both 'since' and 'for' are interchangeable with duration expressions

questions.explanation: ERROR: 'since' is used with a POINT IN TIME (since 2020, since Monday, since morning). 'for' is used with a PERIOD/DURATION (for three years, for two months, for a long time). CORRECT: 'He has been working in this company FOR three years.' SINCE examples: 'I have lived here since 2018.' FOR examples: 'I have lived here for 6 years.' TRICK: Replace with 'starting from ___' (use since) or 'during a span of ___' (use for). 'since three years' is incorrect because three years is a duration, not a point. ALSO CORRECT: 'He has been working here since 2021.' (2021 = point in time). EXAM TRAP: Many candidates use 'since' for duration, especially those who translate from Hindi ('se teen saal se' uses 'se' which resembles 'since'). PYQ FREQUENCY: since vs for error in SSC CGL, IBPS PO English, RRB NTPC — 2-3× per year.

questions.stem: Identify the error in: 'The committee comprising of ten members have submitted their report.'

options.option_text: 'comprising of' and 'have submitted' — 'comprising' needs no 'of'; committee takes singular verb
'The committee' — should be 'A committee' as definite article is wrong here
'their report' — should be 'its report' as the verb is wrong but pronoun is also wrong
No error — 'comprising of' and 'have' are both acceptable in formal British English

questions.explanation: TWO ERRORS: (1) 'COMPRISING OF' is wrong — 'comprise' means to include/consist of and takes a DIRECT OBJECT without 'of.' Write: 'comprising ten members' OR 'composed of ten members.' NEVER 'comprising of.' (2) 'COMMITTEE...HAVE': collective nouns (committee, team, jury, board) take SINGULAR verbs in formal/standard Indian English: 'the committee HAS submitted ITS report.' CORRECT SENTENCE: 'The committee comprising ten members has submitted its report.' RULE FOR COMPRISE: 'The whole comprises the parts' (not 'comprises of the parts'). ALSO: 'The parts compose/constitute the whole.' EXAM TRAP: 'comprising of' sounds natural to many learners but is a grammar error. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'comprising of' error in SSC CGL Tier-1, IBPS PO English — 1-2× per year; collective noun SVA in every exam.

questions.stem: Identify the error in: 'Neither of the two candidates are suitable for the position.'

options.option_text: 'are suitable' — should be 'is suitable'; neither takes a singular verb
'of the two candidates' — 'neither' already implies two; 'two' is redundant but not an error
'for the position' — should be 'to the position' as preposition use is incorrect here
No error — when 'of' is followed by plural noun, plural verb is acceptable by proximity

questions.explanation: ERROR: NEITHER (and EITHER) as a pronoun takes a SINGULAR verb. CORRECT: 'Neither of the two candidates IS suitable.' RULE: Neither/either as pronouns → singular verb (regardless of the plural noun after 'of'). Neither of the boys IS; Either of the girls IS. CONTRAST — CORRELATIVE CONJUNCTION: 'Neither A nor B' with subjects → verb agrees with B (nearer subject): 'Neither Ravi nor his friends ARE coming.' BUT 'Neither of them IS going.' PROXIMITY RULE IS WRONG here — 'of the candidates' does not make the verb plural. OPTION D is wrong: proximity agreement is incorrect in standard grammar. EXAM MEMORY: 'Neither = No + Either = one out of two = singular.' PYQ FREQUENCY: neither/either SVA in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, RRB NTPC English — 1-2× per year.

questions.stem: Identify the error in: 'He insisted that she goes to the meeting without any delay.'

options.option_text: 'she goes' — after 'insist that,' the subjunctive requires base form: 'she go'
'He insisted' — past tense is wrong here; present tense 'insists' should be used instead
'without any delay' — should be 'without no delay' for emphasis in formal English
No error — 'goes' after 'insisted that' follows sequence-of-tenses rules correctly

questions.explanation: ERROR: SUBJUNCTIVE MOOD. After verbs expressing demand/request/suggestion/recommendation (insist, demand, suggest, recommend, propose, require, order), the that-clause uses the BARE INFINITIVE (base form) — NO -s, NO tense inflection. CORRECT: 'He insisted that she GO to the meeting.' Or: 'He insisted that she SHOULD GO.' SUBJUNCTIVE TRIGGERS: insist, demand, suggest, recommend, propose, require, request, order, urge, move (propose a motion). EXAMPLES: 'The doctor suggested that he REST for a week.' 'The court ordered that the defendant APPEAR immediately.' WHY? Subjunctive expresses a hypothetical or mandated state, not a factual one — so no present-tense -s. EXAM TRAP: 'insist + that + she goes' sounds natural because of sequence of tenses confusion, but subjunctive overrides sequence of tenses in such clauses. PYQ FREQUENCY: subjunctive mood error in SSC CGL Tier-2, IBPS PO English — 1× per year.

questions.stem: Identify the error in: 'Having completed the project, a celebration was arranged by the team.'

options.option_text: 'Having completed the project' — dangling participle: the celebration did not complete the project
'a celebration was arranged' — passive voice is incorrect and must be changed to active
'by the team' — 'by' as agent preposition is incorrect and should be 'from the team'
No error — the participial phrase correctly modifies the nearest noun in the sentence

questions.explanation: DANGLING PARTICIPLE ERROR: 'Having completed the project' implies the SUBJECT of the main clause did the completing. But the subject of the main clause is 'a celebration' — celebrations cannot complete projects. The participle DANGLES because its implied subject differs from the sentence's grammatical subject. CORRECT: 'Having completed the project, the team arranged a celebration.' (Now 'team' is the subject and matches 'having completed.') OR: 'After the team completed the project, a celebration was arranged.' RULE: A participial phrase modifies the SUBJECT of the clause that follows it. If the subject doesn't match the action described, it's a dangling modifier. PASSIVE VOICE is NOT the error here (Option B wrong) — passive is fine; the modifier attachment is the problem. PYQ FREQUENCY: dangling participle in SSC CGL Tier-2, IBPS PO Mains English, CAT — 1× per year.

questions.stem: Identify the error in: 'The number of candidates appearing for the examination have increased this year.'

options.option_text: 'have increased' — 'The number of' takes singular verb; should be 'has increased'
'appearing for the examination' — should be 'who appear for the examination' instead
'this year' — should be 'in this year' as a preposition is needed before the time expression
No error — the plural noun 'candidates' after 'of' determines the plural verb correctly

questions.explanation: ERROR: 'THE NUMBER OF + plural noun' takes a SINGULAR verb because the subject is 'the NUMBER' (singular), not the plural noun after 'of.' CORRECT: 'The number of candidates...HAS increased.' CONTRAST: 'A NUMBER OF candidates have applied' — 'a number of' means SEVERAL/MANY and functions as a plural quantifier → PLURAL verb. MEMORY: 'THE number = THE one number → singular. A number = several → plural.' EXAMPLES: 'The number of errors was reduced.' (singular). 'A number of errors were found.' (plural). OPTION D is WRONG: proximity agreement with 'candidates' is an error, not a rule. The grammatical subject is 'The number,' not 'candidates.' PYQ FREQUENCY: 'the number of' vs 'a number of' SVA in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, RRB NTPC English — 1-2× per year.
